## Observations

1. Subtracting \(9(i-1)\) from each \(A_i\) gives a strictly increasing sequence \(B_1,\ldots,B_N\) in \([1,K]\), where \(K=M-9(N-1)\). Adding the offsets back recovers the original sequence and preserves lexicographical order.
2. Every choice of \(N\) distinct integers from \([1,K]\) gives exactly one strictly increasing sequence, so the count is \(\binom{K}{N}\). At the minimum allowed \(M=10N-9\), we have \(K=N\), and there is exactly one sequence.
3. At position \(i\), the next value can range from \(1\) for the first position or \(B_{i-1}+1\) otherwise, up to \(K-(N-i)\). This upper bound leaves enough larger values to complete the sequence.
4. Visiting the choices at each position in ascending order and completing each prefix before moving to the next choice produces lexicographical order. Every prefix generated within the bounds can be completed to at least one output sequence.

## Solution sketch

> Subtracting \(9(i-1)\) from each \(A_i\) gives a strictly increasing sequence \(B_1,\ldots,B_N\) in \([1,K]\), where \(K=M-9(N-1)\). Adding the offsets back recovers the original sequence and preserves lexicographical order.

1. Read \(N\) and \(M\) and compute \(K\). Work in the transformed coordinates because the original gap of at least \(10\) becomes an increase of at least \(1\).

> Every choice of \(N\) distinct integers from \([1,K]\) gives exactly one strictly increasing sequence, so the count is \(\binom{K}{N}\). At the minimum allowed \(M=10N-9\), we have \(K=N\), and there is exactly one sequence.

2. Compute \(X=\binom{K}{N}\) and print it before generating any sequences. When \(K=N\), the enumeration has only one choice at each position and prints \(1,11,\ldots,10N-9\) with spaces between the values.

> At position \(i\), the next value can range from \(1\) for the first position or \(B_{i-1}+1\) otherwise, up to \(K-(N-i)\). This upper bound leaves enough larger values to complete the sequence.

3. Use depth-first backtracking with a single prefix. At position \(i\), try each integer in the allowed range in ascending order. Append it, recurse, and remove it before trying the next candidate. Once the prefix reaches length \(N\), add \(9(i-1)\) back at each position and print the resulting sequence on one space-separated line.

> Visiting the choices at each position in ascending order and completing each prefix before moving to the next choice produces lexicographical order. Every prefix generated within the bounds can be completed to at least one output sequence.

4. Print each sequence as soon as it is complete. Sequences from an earlier branch come first because they have a smaller value at the first position where the branches differ. At any given depth there are at most \(X\) prefixes, since each extends to a distinct output at that depth. Computing the count takes \(O(N)\) arithmetic operations, and generation and printing take \(O(NX)\) time. The prefix and recursion stack use \(O(N)\) auxiliary space.

isolation.mechanism: codex exec, fresh ephemeral session, empty temporary working directory, user config and exec rules ignored, read-only sandbox, web search and listed features disabled, credential-like variables removed from the environment
isolation.limits: Codex harness instructions and its own tool descriptions remain in the model context; they cannot be removed. Tool isolation is verified post hoc from the event stream, which contained no tool, command, file or search events.
